articles.title: How to Ship a Production AI Product with the Claude API
articles.excerpt: A practical roadmap for going from a prompt in a playground to a real AI product in production — architecture, evals, cost control, and the mistakes that stall most teams.
articles.content:
Most AI product ideas die between "the demo worked" and "it's live for real users." The gap isn't the model — it's everything you have to build around it: reliable prompting, evals, cost control, and failure handling. Here's the roadmap that actually gets teams from prototype to production.

1. Start with the failure modes, not the happy path

A prompt that works on your five test cases will break on real user input. Before writing product code, write down:

  • What does "wrong" look like for this feature? (hallucinated fact, wrong format, unsafe content, wrong tone)
  • What's the cost of a wrong answer reaching a user, vs. the cost of a slower/more expensive check?
  • Which failures are cheap to catch with code (JSON schema validation, regex, length checks) vs. which need a second model call or a human?

This determines your architecture more than the prompt does.

2. Separate "prompting" from "product logic"

Keep the parts that talk to Claude thin and swappable. Don't let product logic (billing, permissions, side effects) live inside the same function that constructs prompts. When you inevitably tune the prompt or swap models, you want to touch one layer, not the whole feature.

3. Build evals before you scale traffic

An eval set is just a list of real (input, expected-behavior) pairs you can run automatically. Start small — 20-30 examples pulled from actual usage or support tickets — and run them on every prompt change. Without this, "improving" the prompt for one case silently breaks three others you didn't test.

What to track per eval run:

  • Pass/fail against your own rubric (not just "looks fine")
  • Output format validity (did it parse as the JSON/structure you need?)
  • Latency and token cost per call

4. Design for partial failure, not just total failure

The Claude API will occasionally be slow, rate-limited, or return something your parser doesn't expect. Production-grade AI features handle this explicitly:

  • Retry with backoff on transient errors, not on validation failures
  • A fallback response (cached, templated, or "try again") for when generation fails outright
  • Streaming for anything user-facing that takes more than ~2 seconds, so the UI never looks frozen

5. Control cost the same way you control latency

Token cost scales with context size, and context creep is the most common silent cost leak — a system prompt that grows every time someone "just adds one more instruction," or including full conversation history when a summary would do. Review your actual token usage per request type monthly, not just at launch.

6. Ship behind a flag, watch real usage, then widen

Roll out to a small percentage of real traffic before a full launch. Watch:

  • Eval-style metrics on live traffic, not just your offline test set
  • User-facing signals: retries, edits, abandonment on the AI-powered step
  • Cost per successful outcome, not just cost per API call

If a feature can't clear its eval bar on real traffic, it's not ready to widen — no matter how good it looked in the demo.

This is the same process we walk through, end to end, inside the nextaibuilder cohorts — from a Claude API prototype to something you'd actually trust in front of users.

articles.title: Claude API Prompt Debugging Checklist
articles.excerpt: A free, practical checklist for diagnosing why a Claude API prompt is producing wrong, inconsistent, or malformed output — the questions to ask before you touch the wording.
articles.content:
Save this. When a Claude API prompt starts misbehaving, work through it in order — most "bad prompt" problems are actually one of the first four items, not the wording itself.

1. Is the output actually wrong, or unparsed?

  • Print the raw, unparsed response before your code touches it
  • Check if your parser is stricter than the model's output (e.g. expecting exact JSON but the model added a sentence before it)
  • If you need structured output, are you actually constraining the format (schema, examples, explicit "respond with only JSON")?

2. Is the context actually what you think it is?

  • Log the fully-assembled prompt sent for a failing case — not the template, the real rendered string
  • Check for silently truncated or empty variables (a missing field renders as undefined or blank, and the model will still try to answer)
  • Check token count — is something being cut off by a context limit before the important part?

3. Is the failure input-dependent or consistent?

  • Run the same input 3-5 times. Consistent wrong answer → prompt/context problem. Inconsistent → ambiguity in the prompt, or a task that genuinely needs more structure (few-shot examples, step-by-step instructions).
  • Isolate: does the failure happen with a minimal version of the prompt, or only with your full production context?

4. Are your instructions in tension with each other?

  • List every instruction currently in the system prompt. Do any conflict (e.g. "be concise" + "always explain your reasoning in detail")?
  • Are formatting instructions and behavioral instructions mixed together in a way that could confuse priority?

5. Only now, touch the wording

  • Add 1-3 concrete examples of the exact input/output pattern you want, not just a description of it
  • Move critical constraints to the start or end of the prompt — position matters
  • Change one thing at a time and re-run your eval set (see: How to Ship a Production AI Product with the Claude API) — not just the one failing case

6. If it's still inconsistent

  • Consider whether the task needs decomposition — one call doing five jobs is harder to stabilize than five focused calls
  • Consider whether this specific step needs a human-in-the-loop or a deterministic check instead of a model call at all
More checklists and teardown-style breakdowns like this come out of the nextaibuilder cohorts — see the current cohorts on the homepage.

articles.title: Claude API Tutorial: Your First App in Python & TypeScript
articles.excerpt: A step-by-step Claude API tutorial for beginners: get an API key, install the SDK, send messages, add a system prompt, hold a conversation and stream responses in Python and TypeScript.
articles.content:
Short answer: to call the Claude API, create an API key in the Claude Console, install the official SDK (pip install anthropic or npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk), set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and send a list of messages to client.messages.create() with a model name and max_tokens. The rest of this tutorial walks through each step in Python and TypeScript, then covers system prompts, conversations, streaming and the mistakes beginners hit most.

What you need

  • An Anthropic account and an API key from the Claude Console
  • Python 3.9+ or Node.js 18+
  • About 15 minutes

Step 1: Get an API key and keep it out of your code

Create a key in the Claude Console, then store it as an environment variable. Both SDKs read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY automatically, so the key never appears in your source code or your git history.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

In production, put it in your host's secret manager instead of a .env file that might get committed.

Step 2: Install the SDK

# Python
pip install anthropic

# TypeScript / JavaScript
npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk

Step 3: Send your first message

Python:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain what an API is in two sentences."}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "text":
        print(block.text)

TypeScript:

import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";

const client = new Anthropic(); // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

const response = await client.messages.create({
  model: "claude-opus-5-5",
  max_tokens: 1024,
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Explain what an API is in two sentences." }],
});

for (const block of response.content) {
  if (block.type === "text") console.log(block.text);
}

The response's content is a list of blocks, not a single string. Check each block's type before reading text; later, when you add tools, the same list also holds tool calls.

Step 4: Add a system prompt

The system parameter sets the role, rules and output format for the whole conversation. Keep product rules here rather than repeating them in every user message.

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a support assistant for an online course. Answer in plain English, under 120 words.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Can I pay in installments?"}],
)

Step 5: Hold a conversation

The API is stateless: it remembers nothing between calls. To continue a conversation, send the earlier turns back with each request, alternating user and assistant.

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Suggest a name for a habit-tracking app."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "How about Streakly?"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Give me three more in the same style."},
]
response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=messages)

Long conversations get expensive because every call resends the history. Summarise or trim old turns once a conversation grows.

Step 6: Stream the answer

For anything a user waits on, stream the text so it appears word by word instead of after a long pause.

with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a short welcome email for new students."}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)

Choosing a model

  • Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5): the most capable; use it for complex reasoning, coding and agents.
  • Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5): a strong balance of quality and cost for most product features.
  • Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5): the fastest and cheapest; good for classification, routing and high-volume tasks.

Start with the most capable model while you build, measure quality with a small set of test cases, then try a cheaper model and keep it only if those tests still pass.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Reading content[0].text blindly. The first block is not always text. Loop over blocks and check the type.
  • Setting max_tokens too low. If stop_reason is max_tokens, the answer was cut off; raise the limit or ask for shorter output.
  • Hardcoding the API key. Use the environment variable, and rotate any key that was ever committed.
  • Writing your own retry loop. The SDKs already retry rate limits (429) and server errors with backoff.
  • No tests for prompts. Keep 20 to 30 real inputs and rerun them on every prompt change. Our prompt debugging checklist shows what to check.

Where to go next

Once single calls work, the next step is letting Claude use tools, which turns a chatbot into an agent. Read how to build an AI agent with Claude, then MCP explained to connect it to real systems, and how to ship a production AI product for evals, cost control and launch.

If you want to build a complete product with guidance, the live cohort covers all of this over five weeks, and the self-paced course lets you follow the same curriculum on your own schedule.

FAQ

Is the Claude API free?

No. The API is billed per token, separately from a Claude.ai chat subscription. New accounts can check the Claude Console for any available credits.

What is the difference between Claude.ai and the Claude API?

Claude.ai is the chat app for people. The Claude API is for developers who want to call Claude from their own code and build it into a product.

Which programming languages are supported?

Anthropic publishes official SDKs for Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C# and PHP. Any language can also call the HTTP API directly.

What does max_tokens mean?

It is the maximum length of Claude's reply, in tokens. It does not limit the input. If a reply hits the limit, it is cut off and stop_reason is max_tokens.

articles.title: How to Build an AI Agent with Claude, Step by Step
articles.excerpt: Build a working AI agent with the Claude API: define tools, write the agent loop, handle tool errors and add the guardrails you need before real users touch it.
articles.content:
Short answer: an AI agent is a loop. You give Claude a goal and a set of tools described as JSON schemas. Claude replies either with an answer or with a request to call a tool; your code runs the tool, sends the result back, and repeats until Claude says it is done. This guide builds that loop step by step with the Claude API in Python.

Chatbot vs agent

A chatbot answers from what it already knows. An agent can act: look up an order, read a file, create a ticket, then decide what to do next based on the result. The model chooses which tool to call and when; your code decides which tools exist and what they are allowed to do.

Step 1: Define a tool

A tool has a name, a description and an input schema. The description is what Claude reads to decide when to use it, so write it like documentation for a new teammate.

tools = [
    {
        "name": "get_order_status",
        "description": "Look up the shipping status of a customer order by its order ID. Use this whenever the customer asks where their order is.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "The order ID, e.g. A-1042"}
            },
            "required": ["order_id"],
        },
    }
]

def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    # Replace with a real database or API call.
    return f"Order {order_id} shipped yesterday and arrives Friday."

Step 2: Write the agent loop

Call the API with the tools. If the reply's stop_reason is tool_use, run each requested tool, send the results back as tool_result blocks, and call again. Stop when Claude finishes.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is my order A-1042?"}]

while True:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=4096,
        system="You are a support agent for an online store. Use tools to check facts before answering.",
        tools=tools,
        messages=messages,
    )
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break

    results = []
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            if block.name == "get_order_status":
                output = get_order_status(**block.input)
            else:
                output = f"Unknown tool: {block.name}"
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

print(next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

Three details matter here. Each tool_result must carry the tool_use_id of the call it answers. Claude can request several tools in one reply, so handle every tool_use block, not just the first. And the whole history, including tool calls and results, goes back on every turn.

The Python and TypeScript SDKs also include a tool runner (currently in beta) that runs this loop for you from decorated functions. Writing the loop once by hand is still the best way to understand what the runner does.

Step 3: Handle errors as results, not crashes

When a tool fails, return the error to Claude as the tool result, with "is_error": true, instead of raising an exception. Claude can then retry with different input or explain the problem to the user.

results.append({
    "type": "tool_result",
    "tool_use_id": block.id,
    "content": "Order not found. Ask the customer to check the ID.",
    "is_error": True,
})

Step 4: Add guardrails before real users

  • Cap the loop. Stop after a fixed number of turns (for example 10) so a confused agent cannot run up cost.
  • Separate read and write tools. Let the agent read freely, but require confirmation, or a human, before tools that send email, charge money or delete data.
  • Validate tool input in code. Never trust the model to stay inside limits you can check yourself, such as refund amounts or allowed IDs.
  • Log every tool call. When something goes wrong, the tool-call log is how you find out why.
  • Test with real cases. Run 20 to 30 real requests on every change and check both the final answer and which tools were called.

Designing good tools

  • Prefer a few focused tools over one tool with a dozen modes.
  • Return short, structured results. Dumping a whole database row wastes tokens and confuses the model.
  • Say in the description when not to use the tool, as well as when to use it.
  • Name inputs the way your users talk ("order_id", not "oid").

From one agent to real integrations

Writing a tool definition for every system gets repetitive. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) packages tools for systems like GitHub, Jira or Slack as reusable servers that any MCP client can use. Read MCP explained next. If you are new to the API itself, start with the Claude API tutorial.

Designing agents, connecting them to Jira, Confluence, Slack and GitHub, and testing them with quality gates are weeks 2 to 4 of the live cohort, where you build an agent for your own product.

FAQ

What is the difference between tool use and function calling?

They are the same idea. Anthropic calls it tool use: you describe functions, the model asks to call them, and your code runs them.

Does Claude run my tools itself?

No. For tools you define, Claude only asks for a call with specific inputs; your code runs the function and returns the result. Anthropic also offers server tools, such as web search, that run on its side.

How many tools can an agent have?

There is no small fixed limit, but quality drops when many similar tools compete. Start with the few tools the task needs and add more only when tests show a gap.

Which Claude model is best for agents?

Use the most capable model, currently Claude Opus 5.5, while you build and test. Once your tests pass, try a cheaper model for simpler agents and keep it only if the tests still pass.

articles.title: MCP Explained: Connect Claude to Your Tools
articles.excerpt: What the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is, how MCP servers and clients work, how to connect a server to Claude Code, and how to build a small MCP server in Python.
articles.content:
Short answer: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server wraps a system such as GitHub, Jira, a database or your own API and exposes its actions as tools. An MCP client, such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop, connects to the server so Claude can use those tools. Build the integration once as a server and every MCP client can use it.

Why MCP exists

Before MCP, every AI app needed its own custom code for every integration: one connector for Slack in this app, another for Slack in that one. MCP standardises the connection, the same way USB standardised plugging devices into computers. Tool builders write one server; AI apps speak one protocol.

The three building blocks

  • Tools: actions the model can call, such as "create a Jira issue" or "search the codebase". These are the most used part of MCP.
  • Resources: read-only data the client can load into context, such as a file, a document or a database schema.
  • Prompts: reusable prompt templates the server offers, such as "review this pull request".

How a request flows

  1. The client starts or connects to the MCP server and asks which tools it offers.
  2. The client passes those tool descriptions to Claude along with the user's request.
  3. Claude decides to call a tool; the client forwards the call to the server.
  4. The server runs it against the real system and returns the result, which goes back to Claude.

This is the same tool-use loop described in how to build an AI agent with Claude; MCP standardises where the tools come from.

Local and remote servers

  • Local (stdio): the client starts the server as a process on your machine and talks to it over standard input and output. Good for developer tools and files on your computer.
  • Remote (HTTP): the server runs as a web service, usually behind OAuth. Good for SaaS products and shared team tools.

Connect an MCP server to Claude Code

Claude Code adds servers with the claude mcp add command. For a remote server:

claude mcp add --transport http my-server https://example.com/mcp

For a local server, put the command that starts it after --:

claude mcp add my-tools -- python server.py

Run claude mcp list to check the connection, then ask Claude to use the new tools in plain English.

Build a tiny MCP server in Python

The official MCP Python SDK turns ordinary functions into tools. Install it with pip install mcp, then:

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("course-tools")

@mcp.tool()
def next_cohort_date() -> str:
    """Return the start date of the next live cohort."""
    return "The next cohort starts on the date listed on the course page."

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()  # stdio by default

The function's name, type hints and docstring become the tool's name, input schema and description, so write the docstring for the model: say what the tool does and when to use it.

Security: treat MCP servers like code you install

  • Only connect servers from sources you trust; a server can run commands with your permissions.
  • Give each server the smallest access it needs, such as a read-only token where possible.
  • Be careful with servers that read untrusted content (web pages, emails, tickets). That content can contain instructions aimed at the model, so keep write actions behind confirmation.
  • Review what a server's tools can change before letting an agent call them without asking.

MCP vs plain tool use

If a tool exists only inside one product, defining it directly with the API's tools parameter is simpler. Reach for MCP when the same integration should work in several clients, when you want to reuse existing servers for GitHub, Jira or Slack, or when you want teammates to plug the same tools into Claude Code.

Week 2 of the live cohort covers tool use and the MCP pattern, and week 3 connects agents to Jira, Confluence, Slack and GitHub. New to the API? Start with the Claude API tutorial.

FAQ

Is MCP only for Claude?

No. MCP is an open protocol. Anthropic created it, and other AI tools and clients also support it.

Do I need MCP to use tools with the Claude API?

No. You can define tools directly in an API request. MCP is useful when you want reusable integrations that work across clients.

What is the difference between an MCP server and an API?

An API is how a system exposes its features to programs. An MCP server wraps one or more APIs and describes them as tools in a standard format that AI clients understand.

Which language should I write an MCP server in?

Official SDKs exist for several languages, including Python and TypeScript. Use the one your team already works in.

articles.title: Claude Code vs Cursor: Which AI Coding Tool Should You Use?
articles.excerpt: Claude Code vs Cursor compared: who drives each step, when each tool fits, the features that matter on real projects, and a workflow that uses both.
articles.content:
Short answer: Cursor is an AI code editor: you stay in the editor and get fast autocomplete, inline edits and a chat or agent panel next to your code. Claude Code is an agent from Anthropic that works on your whole repository from the terminal (and from IDE extensions, a desktop app and the web): you describe a task, it plans, edits many files, runs commands and tests, and reports back. Most teams that ship with AI use both: Cursor for moment-to-moment editing, Claude Code for larger tasks you can hand off.

The real difference: who drives

The useful way to compare them is not feature lists, which change every month, but who is in control of each step.

  • In Cursor, you drive. You open a file, accept or reject a suggestion, highlight a block and ask for a change. AI makes each step faster, but you decide what happens next.
  • In Claude Code, the agent drives. You give it a goal such as "add rate limiting to the API and write tests", and it reads the code, decides which files to change, runs the test suite and iterates until the task is done or it needs your input. You review the result as a diff.

Both tools now overlap: Cursor has an agent mode, and Claude Code runs inside VS Code and JetBrains. But their defaults still reflect these two styles, and that is what decides which one fits a task.

When Cursor is the better fit

  • Small, frequent edits where you already know what to change: renaming, refactoring a function, fixing a type error.
  • Writing new code line by line, where tab autocomplete saves the most time.
  • Exploring an unfamiliar file with quick questions in a side chat while you read.
  • Front-end work where you want to see each change and tweak it immediately.

When Claude Code is the better fit

  • Multi-file tasks: a feature that touches the API, the database and the UI.
  • Work that needs commands: running tests, migrations, linters or a build, and fixing what fails.
  • Spec-first development: write a short spec in a file like docs/PRD.md, ask Claude Code to implement it with tests first, then review the diff.
  • Automation: Claude Code can run non-interactively in scripts and CI, for example to triage failing tests or draft a pull request.
  • Connecting real tools: through MCP servers it can read Jira tickets, Confluence pages, GitHub issues or Figma designs while it works.

Features that matter for real projects

Project memory. Claude Code reads a CLAUDE.md file in your repository on every session: coding conventions, commands, architecture notes. Cursor has an equivalent in project rules. Whichever you use, writing these down is the single biggest quality improvement, because the agent stops guessing your conventions.

Customisation. Claude Code supports custom slash commands, skills, subagents for parallel work, and hooks that run your own scripts before or after actions (for example, a formatter after every edit). Cursor offers rules, custom modes and its own MCP support.

Models. Claude Code runs on Anthropic's Claude models. Cursor lets you choose between several providers, including Claude.

Review. With either tool, the output is a diff you are responsible for. Treat it like a pull request from a fast junior engineer: read it, run it, and ask for tests.

A workflow that uses both

  1. Write a one-page spec for the feature: the goal, the user stories and the acceptance criteria.
  2. Ask Claude Code to read the spec, propose a plan and implement it with tests first.
  3. Review the diff. For small fixes, edit directly in Cursor with autocomplete and inline edits.
  4. Ask Claude Code to run the full test suite and fix anything that broke.
  5. Open the pull request and let a review step, human or agent, check it before merge.

This is the workflow taught in week 1 of the live cohort, and it scales from a weekend project to a team codebase.

How to choose if you can only pick one

  • You write most code yourself and want it faster: start with Cursor.
  • You want to hand off whole tasks, work from specs, or you are a product person building without writing every line: start with Claude Code.
  • You are building an AI product, not just using AI to code: learn the Claude API as well, because your product will call the model directly.

FAQ

Is Claude Code better than Cursor?

Neither is better in general. Cursor is stronger for fast, hands-on editing inside an editor; Claude Code is stronger for multi-file tasks, running commands and handing off whole features. Many developers use both.

Can I use Claude models in Cursor?

Yes. Cursor lets you choose between several model providers, and Claude models are among them.

Does Claude Code work inside VS Code?

Yes. Claude Code runs in the terminal and also has extensions for VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, plus a desktop app and a web version.

Do I need to know how to code to use Claude Code?

It helps, because you are responsible for reviewing what it changes. But product managers and founders do use it to build working products when they pair it with a clear spec and tests.

What is CLAUDE.md?

A Markdown file in your repository that Claude Code reads at the start of every session. Put your conventions, common commands and architecture notes there so the agent follows them without being told each time.

articles.title: Prompt Caching with the Claude API: Cut Costs and Latency
articles.excerpt: How Claude prompt caching works, how to add cache_control in Python, how to check it is working, what it costs, and the mistakes that silently break it.
articles.content:
Short answer: prompt caching lets the Claude API reuse the processed start of a prompt across requests. You mark a point in the prompt with cache_control; the first request writes everything up to that point to the cache, and later requests with the exact same prefix read it back at a fraction of the normal input price and with lower latency. It pays off whenever many requests share a long, stable beginning: a big system prompt, tool definitions, a document, or a growing conversation.

How prompt caching works

Caching is a prefix match. The API renders your request in a fixed order, tools first, then system, then messages, and caches the exact bytes up to each breakpoint you mark. If a single character changes anywhere before a breakpoint, that breakpoint and everything after it miss the cache.

That one rule explains almost every caching problem: put what never changes first, what changes per user or session next, and what changes on every request last.

Add caching in Python

The simplest option is automatic caching: a top-level cache_control caches up to the last cacheable block of the request.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},  # cache up to the last cacheable block
    system=LONG_PRODUCT_MANUAL,             # the same text on every request
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I reset my password?"}],
)
print(response.usage)

For control over where the cache ends, put cache_control on a specific content block instead. Here the long, shared manual is cached and the question after it is not:

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": LONG_PRODUCT_MANUAL,
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},  # 5-minute cache by default
        }
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
)

In TypeScript the request has the same shape: pass cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" } on the block, or at the top level of client.messages.create().

Check that it is working

Every response reports cache activity in usage:

  • cache_creation_input_tokens: tokens written to the cache by this request.
  • cache_read_input_tokens: tokens read from the cache instead of being processed again.
  • input_tokens: the remaining, uncached input.

Send the same request twice. The first should show a cache write; the second, a cache read. If both show zero, the cached part is probably shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length (it ranges from about 512 to 4,096 tokens depending on the model). Short prefixes are simply not cached, and there is no error.

What it costs, and when it pays off

  • Cache reads cost a small fraction of the normal input price (around a tenth on most models, less on some newer ones).
  • Cache writes cost more than normal input: 1.25 times for the default 5-minute cache, 2 times for the 1-hour cache.
  • With the 5-minute cache, two requests that share a prefix already break even. With the 1-hour cache you need at least three.

Each read refreshes the timer, so steady traffic keeps a 5-minute cache warm indefinitely. Use the 1-hour option only when requests sharing a prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart. Check current per-model prices on Anthropic's pricing page before estimating savings.

Where to put breakpoints

  • Large system prompt or tool list: one breakpoint on the last system block. Tools render before the system prompt, so both are cached together.
  • Chat and agent conversations: a breakpoint on the last block of the newest turn. Each new request reuses the whole earlier conversation.
  • Shared document, different questions: a breakpoint at the end of the document, not at the end of the question. Otherwise every request writes its own entry and nothing is ever read back.

You can use up to four breakpoints per request.

The mistakes that silently break caching

  • A timestamp or date in the system prompt. The prefix changes every request. Pass the date later, in a user message.
  • User names or IDs interpolated into the system prompt. Every user gets a separate cache. Keep the system prompt identical for everyone.
  • Tools built per user or in random order. Tools come first in the prompt, so any difference invalidates everything. Sort them by name and keep the set fixed.
  • JSON serialised without a stable key order. The same data produces different bytes. Sort keys.
  • Switching models mid-conversation. Caches belong to one model.

Caching pairs well with the other cost levers in our production guide: right-sized models, shorter outputs and batching for work that is not urgent. In an agent loop, where every step resends the conversation so far, caching is often the biggest single saving.

FAQ

How much does prompt caching save?

Cached input is billed at a small fraction of the normal input price, around a tenth on most models, so savings on the cached part can approach 90%. Your real saving depends on how much of each request is a shared prefix and how often it is reused.

How long does the Claude prompt cache last?

Five minutes by default, refreshed every time the cache is read. You can ask for a one-hour cache with "ttl": "1h", which costs more to write.

Why is my prompt not being cached?

The usual causes are a prefix shorter than the model minimum, something that changes in the prefix on every request (a timestamp, an ID, unsorted JSON, a different tool list), or a breakpoint placed after content that varies per request.

Does prompt caching change the answers?

No. Caching only skips reprocessing an identical prefix; the model sees the same prompt and responds the same way.

Is the cache shared between customers?

No. Caches are isolated to your organization (per workspace on the Claude API) and are never shared with other organizations.

articles.title: How to Evaluate an AI Agent: A Practical Guide to Evals
articles.excerpt: Build an eval for your AI feature or agent: collect realistic cases, choose code checks or a model judge, grade outcomes and tool calls, and read the score honestly.
articles.content:
Short answer: an eval is a repeatable test for an AI feature. It has three parts: a set of realistic inputs, a script that runs your app on each one, and a grader that scores each output. Run it before and after every change to a prompt, model or tool, and you replace "it seems better" with a number you can trust. For agents, grade the outcome the user cares about, and check the steps the agent took on the way.

Why AI features need evals

Traditional tests check that code returns an exact value. Model output varies, so the same prompt can pass on Monday and fail on Tuesday, and a small prompt change can fix one case while breaking three others. Without an eval you only find out from users. With one, every change gets a score before it ships.

Step 1: Collect the inputs

Use the most realistic source you have, in this order:

  1. Real traffic. Logs or transcripts of what users actually send. Remove personal data first.
  2. Things that went wrong. Bug reports, support tickets and the cases someone complained about. These are the most valuable.
  3. Hand-written cases. Ask the people who know the domain for ten examples, including the hard ones.
  4. Synthetic variations of those real examples, to fill gaps. Do not invent cases from nothing; they come out too easy.

Start with 15 to 100 cases. Fewer than 15 and one flaky case swings the score; far more and nobody reviews them. Read every case before you use it.

Step 2: Decide how to grade

  • Code checks where the answer is objective: valid JSON, the right category, a number in range, the expected tool called. Cheap, fast and exact.
  • A model as judge for qualities like correctness, tone or completeness. Give the judge a short rubric with pass and fail examples, ask for a verdict plus a reason, and spot-check its grades against your own.
  • Human review for a sample, especially early on, to confirm the automated grades mean what you think.

Grade outcomes, not wording. "Did the reply give the correct refund window?" is a good check; "does the reply match this exact sentence?" fails good answers.

Step 3: Evaluating agents

An agent takes several steps and calls tools, so grade at two levels:

  • Outcome: did the task get done? The ticket was created with the right fields, the answer is correct, the file contains the fix.
  • Trajectory: did it get there safely? It called the right tools, never called a forbidden one, did not loop, and stayed within a step and cost budget.

Tools with real side effects, such as sending email or writing to a database, should be replaced with test versions during evals. Record the calls the agent makes and grade those instead.

Step 4: A minimal eval runner

This Python script runs a support assistant on each case and uses Claude as a judge with a simple rubric. Replace answer() with a call to your real app.

import json
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"

CASES = [
    {"input": "Can I get a refund after 3 weeks?", "expect": "Refunds are within 2 weeks; politely say no and offer help."},
    {"input": "Can I pay in installments?", "expect": "Yes, 3 monthly payments."},
]

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    """Your app. Replace with the real entry point."""
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=512,
        system="You are the support assistant for an online course. Answer briefly.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    )
    return "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")

def judge(question: str, expect: str, reply: str) -> dict:
    rubric = (
        "Grade the reply. PASS only if it is consistent with the expected behaviour "
        "and contains no invented facts. Respond with JSON: "
        '{"verdict": "PASS" or "FAIL", "reason": "one sentence"}'
    )
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=200,
        system=rubric,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Question: {question}\nExpected: {expect}\nReply: {reply}"}],
    )
    text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    return json.loads(text[text.find("{"): text.rfind("}") + 1])

passed = 0
for case in CASES:
    reply = answer(case["input"])
    grade = judge(case["input"], case["expect"], reply)
    passed += grade["verdict"] == "PASS"
    print(grade["verdict"], "|", case["input"], "|", grade["reason"])

print(f"{passed}/{len(CASES)} passed")

Save every run's inputs, outputs, grades, token usage and cost to a file, so you can compare runs and read the failures, not just the score.

Step 5: Read the number honestly

  • Run each case more than once. Model output varies, so one run can mislead. With 25 cases run twice, a pass rate is only accurate to roughly ±14 percentage points; small differences between two prompts are noise.
  • Keep a held-out set. If you tune a prompt against the same cases you measure on, you will overfit. Keep some cases aside and check them only at the end.
  • Watch cost and latency too. A prompt that scores two points higher but doubles the tokens may not be worth it.
  • Check for truncation. If a response stopped at max_tokens, the grade reflects the limit, not the model.

When a case fails, our prompt debugging checklist helps find out why before you change the wording.

Make it part of shipping

Run the eval on every prompt, model or tool change, and in CI for anything that reaches users. Add each new production failure as a case. Over time the eval becomes the most valuable asset in your AI feature: it is what lets you upgrade models and change prompts with confidence. Building these quality gates is week 4 of the live cohort and the self-paced course.

FAQ

What is an LLM eval?

A repeatable test for a feature that uses a language model: a set of inputs, a way to run your app on each, and a grader that scores the outputs, so you can measure whether a change made things better or worse.

How many test cases do I need?

Start with 15 to 100 realistic cases. Fewer makes the score jumpy; many more is fine later, but only if someone still reads the failures.

Can I use Claude to grade Claude?

Yes, a model-as-judge works well for qualities that code cannot check, if you give it a clear rubric, ask for a reason with each verdict, and compare a sample of its grades with your own.

How do I evaluate an AI agent?

Grade the final outcome the user cares about, and separately check the trajectory: which tools were called, whether any forbidden action happened, and whether it stayed within a step and cost budget. Replace tools that have side effects with test versions.

How often should I run evals?

On every change to a prompt, model, tool or retrieval setup, and before every release of the feature.

steps.title: Install Homebrew
steps.content:
Homebrew is a package manager for Mac that makes installing developer tools simple. You'll use it to install Node.js in the next step.

1.1 Open Terminal - Press Command (⌘) + Space to open Spotlight Search - Type Terminal and press Enter

1.2 Install Homebrew Copy and paste this entire command into Terminal, then press Enter:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
  • You may be asked to enter your Mac login password — type it and press Enter (nothing shows on screen — this is normal)
  • The installation will take 2–5 minutes

1.3 Add Homebrew to Your PATH (Apple Silicon Macs only) If your Mac has an Apple Silicon chip (M1, M2, M3, M4), run these two commands:

echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile

eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"

1.4 Verify Homebrew Installed

brew --version

You should see something like: Homebrew 5.x.x
steps.criteria: Screenshot should show a Terminal window with the output of `brew --version` displaying a version number like "Homebrew 5.x.x". The Terminal prompt should be visible.

steps.title: Install Node.js
steps.content:
Node.js is the runtime required to run Claude Code. Install it using Homebrew.

Install Node.js

brew install node

Verify Node.js Installed

node --version
npm --version

You should see version numbers for both Node.js (v18 or later) and npm.
steps.criteria: Screenshot should show a Terminal window with the output of both `node --version` and `npm --version` commands displaying version numbers. Node.js should be v18 or later.

steps.title: Install Claude Code
steps.content:
Install the Claude Code CLI globally using npm.

Install Claude Code

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Fix Permissions (only if you get a permission error)

sudo npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Verify Claude Code Installed

claude --version

You should see a version number confirming Claude Code is installed.
steps.criteria: Screenshot should show a Terminal window with the output of `claude --version` displaying a version number. The command should run without any errors.

steps.title: Authenticate with Your Anthropic Account
steps.content:
Connect Claude Code to your Anthropic account to start using it.

4.1 Create an Anthropic Account (if you don't have one)

Go to https://console.anthropic.com and sign up for a free account.

4.2 Log In to Claude Code

claude

The first time you run this, Claude Code will open your browser and ask you to log in.

  1. Log in with your Anthropic account credentials
  2. Click "Authorize" or "Allow"
  3. Return to Terminal — you should see a welcome message from Claude

You are now set up and ready to use Claude Code!
steps.criteria: Screenshot should show a Terminal window with Claude Code running and displaying a welcome message after successful authentication. The Terminal should show the Claude Code prompt or a confirmation that you are logged in.
